card.title: Bohr energy levels and the spectral lines they explain

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Hydrogen's electron can occupy only the fixed levels Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV. Light appears only when it drops to a lower level, which is why the spectrum is a set of sharp lines instead of a continuous band.

figure.caption: Hydrogen levels and the n = 3 → 2 jump that emits the 656 nm H-alpha photon.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV;  1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²);  ΔE = hν = hc/λ;  R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Exact only for one-electron species such as H and He⁺; every transition has Δn ≠ 0 and the photon carries exactly E_high − E_low.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: n = 3 → 2 gives the red 656 nm H-alpha line of the Balmer series; the Lyman series lies in the ultraviolet and its limit is the 13.6 eV ionisation energy.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: It cannot explain line splitting in a magnetic field or any multi-electron spectrum, and it keeps the definite orbit that quantum mechanics replaces with an orbital.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: mv r = nh/2π with mv²/r = Ze²/(4πε₀r²) ⇒ r = 0.529 n²/Z Å and E = −13.6 Z²/n² eV;  then hc/λ = E₂ − E₁

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: λ(nm) = 1240 / ΔE(eV) skips every unit conversion; for hydrogen λ(Å) = 1216.3 n₁²n₂²/(n₂² − n₁²).

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Draw the energy-level diagram of hydrogen and explain how the Balmer series is produced.
